extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and creative writers interested in literary aesthetics and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts from a literary-philosophical work that articulate principles for literary creation and judgement—emphasizing authenticity, matter, clarity, attentiveness, and how to relate to past styles. Useful as aesthetic guidance for writers and critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept historical/intellectual difference in literary function
rubrics_metrics.description: “A true literary tact would accept that difference in forming the primary conception of the literary function at a later time.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or attempting to revive earlier modes, recognise that the intellectual conditions of another age differ fundamentally. Critical tact requires taking that difference as primary rather than forcing earlier standards onto later work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid artificial novitas or contrived naïveté
rubrics_metrics.description: “Perhaps the utmost one could get by conscious effort, in the way of a reaction or return to the conditions of an earlier and fresher age, would be but novitas, artificial artlessness, naïveté.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consciously imitating the freshness of an earlier period tends to produce an artificial petit charm rather than genuine vitality. Such ‘novitas’ may have superficial charm (a euphuistic effect) but should not be mistaken for authentic early freshness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive matter (real subject) saves mannerism
rubrics_metrics.description: Flavian was ‘saved by the consciousness that he had a matter to present, very real, at least to him.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even elaborate manner or stylistic affectation can be redeemed if the writer has genuine matter—an authentic personal subject or vision. Prioritise substantive content grounded in the author's own conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let form serve sincere personal intuitions (faithful clothing of the model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form and assiduous cultivation of manner should bring to the surface “certain strong personal intuitions... which the artistic or literary faculty was called upon to follow, with the exactness of wax or clay, clothing the model within.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft should be precise and serve to embody inner vision. Avoid allowing ornamental or mannered form to overshadow or falsify the underlying intuition; aim for fidelity between inner perception and its formal expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when you are genuinely interested—interest others by genuine interest
rubrics_metrics.description: “To know when one’s self is interested, is the first condition of interesting other people.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select material and emotional investment honestly: a writer’s authentic engagement with subject-matter is the primary means of engaging readers. Anti-pattern: feigned or complacent sentiment undertaken merely to please an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrupulous literary sincerity and selective intellectual diet
rubrics_metrics.description: Flavian’s ‘jealous and fastidious in the selection of his intellectual food; often listless while others read... never pretending to be moved out of mere complaisance to people’s emotions... foster in him a very scrupulous literary sincerity with himself.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be fastidious in what you read and absorb; cultivate sincerity toward your own tastes and avoid affectation. This inward honesty shapes authentic writing and protects against fashionable insincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firmness of outline and mastery of practical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Marius prized in Flavian a ‘firmness of outline... like that of some master of noble metal-work, manipulating tenacious bronze or gold.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value structural clarity and strong, well-defined form—analogous to the solidity and precision of metalwork. A firm outline gives work endurance and resistence to mere prettiness; craftsmanship of effect matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance traditional richness with novel sound and cadence
rubrics_metrics.description: Flavian retained ‘the opulent, many-syllabled vocabulary of the Latin genius’ yet ‘had caught something of the rhyming cadence... of the medieval Latin’—anticipating ‘wholly new laws of taste as regards sound.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovate in sound and rhythm while respecting substantive strengths of tradition. Effective work can combine the richness of inherited language with new auditory patterns; sound is a vector of aesthetic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic beauty in clearness of thought (austerity of mind as aesthetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: There was ‘a poetic beauty in mere clearness of thought, the actually aesthetic charm of a cold austerity of mind.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity and intellectual austerity are themselves aesthetic virtues. Avoid mistaking theatrical mysticism or sentimental excess for profundity; clear thinking can produce powerful poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual scrupulousness and scepticism toward theatrical mysticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Marius was kept ‘by a genuine virility... as a hatred of what was theatrical, and the instinctive recognition that in vigorous intelligence... divinity was most likely to be found a resident.’ He was ‘instinctively suspicious of those mechanical arcana, those pretended ‘secrets unveiled’ of the professional mystic.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise scepticism toward ready-made mystical formulas and theatrical revelations. Value vigorous intelligence and honest inquiry over contrived spiritualism; avoid lowering intellect to the level of ‘professional mystic’ tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-knowledge and precise orientation of creative intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: He sought ‘to determine his bearings, as by compass, in the world of thought—to get that precise acquaintance with the creative intelligence itself, its structure and capacities... An exact estimate of realities... a delicately measured gradation of certainty in things.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should cultivate self-knowledge and intellectual discipline—know the limits of imagination versus fact, and measure degrees of certainty. No disguises: precise internal orientation strengthens creative authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict attentiveness: correct sense by reason, deny habitual impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Heraclitus: the appeal ‘from confused to unconfused sensation’; ‘the many... are like people heavy with wine... much learning doth not make wise...’ and ‘strict attentiveness of mind a kind of religious duty and service.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject passive, habitual perception; cultivate careful, correcting attention. Train perception by reason so that fleeting sensory impressions do not mislead—attentiveness is both an intellectual and aesthetic discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apprehend flux but seek intelligible relations (harmony in mutation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heraclitus’s doctrine: things are in perpetual change, yet there is a ‘continuance... of orderly intelligible relationships, like the harmony of musical notes, wrought out in and through the series of their mutations.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise transience and flux but look for enduring intelligible patterns and harmonies within change. The aesthetic task includes finding order and relation amid motion rather than yielding to despair that knowledge is impossible.
